segments.desc: Civic-minded citizens who believe government accountability is essential and that the public has a right to know how local funds are spent, reflecting the strong sentiment that government should serve the people rather than act as their boss.

Community members who have had frustrating experiences trying to access government information and see budget transparency as a basic democratic right, even if they rarely contact their councillors directly.
Traditional or authority-deferential residents who view some government information as appropriately restricted and trust officials to manage finances without public scrutiny.
Uncertain or disengaged citizens who are unsure about the boundaries of public information rights and may not have strong opinions either way.

Frustrated citizens who feel the government has consistently failed to adequately equip health facilities, citing long-standing shortages of medicines, equipment, and staff that were exposed by COVID-19
Moderately critical Kenyans who acknowledge some government effort in procuring PPE and setting up isolation centers but feel the response was too slow and uneven across regions
Cautiously satisfied residents, often in urban areas near better-resourced hospitals, who saw tangible improvements in health facility capacity during the pandemic
Strong government supporters who believe the Kenyan government did a commendable job mobilizing resources for health facilities given the country's economic constraints
Disengaged or uncertain citizens who did not closely follow health facility conditions during COVID-19 and have no strong opinion

Ordinary Kenyans who feel disconnected from local government and have never reached out to a councillor, either because they don't know how, don't trust the process, or don't believe it would make a difference based on past experiences with unresponsive institutions.
Rural residents and urban poor who are too preoccupied with daily survival struggles like finding cash income and medicines to engage in civic outreach to local officials.
Civically engaged citizens who have contacted their local councillor once or a few times, usually around a specific community issue like infrastructure or service delivery.
Active community members or local leaders who regularly engage with their councillor and see it as an effective channel for voicing concerns and influencing local decisions.

Skeptical citizens who have had poor experiences with local government responsiveness and believe officials are unlikely to share budget or planning information with ordinary people, seeing bureaucracy as opaque and self-serving.
Moderately hopeful residents who think it is somewhat possible to get such information, especially given recent reforms and Morocco's stated commitments to transparency, though they remain cautious.
Optimistic or civically engaged individuals, often younger or urban, who believe local government offices are accessible and that development plan information can be obtained if you know how to ask.
Rural or less educated citizens who have little experience interacting with local government offices and genuinely don't know how likely it would be to get such information.
Deeply disillusioned citizens who see local government as entirely closed off and believe it is not at all likely that any meaningful budget or planning information would be shared with the public.

Democratic-minded citizens who strongly support Cabo Verde's stable democratic tradition and see military rule as a threat to the freedoms and institutions they value, disapproving strongly of army governance.
Younger educated urbanites who are aware of military coups in other African nations and view army rule as incompatible with development and good governance, disapproving of this option.

Disillusioned citizens who are deeply frustrated with Parliament (as shown by the high disapproval of MPs) and might see military intervention as a possible corrective, approving or remaining neutral.
Politically indifferent or uncertain individuals who have little strong opinion on governance structures and would neither approve nor disapprove or say they don't know.
Government supporters who strongly approve of the President and trust state institutions, believing the government will ensure vaccine safety as part of its duty to citizens.
Moderately trusting citizens who are fairly satisfied with government COVID-19 responses and give the government some benefit of the doubt on vaccine safety, though not unconditionally.
Skeptics who see corruption as increasing and distrust government competence or honesty, doubting the government's ability to guarantee vaccine safety.
Traditional and community-oriented individuals who trust traditional leaders more than formal government institutions and are uncertain about government vaccine oversight.
Disengaged or uninformed citizens who don't follow government health policy closely and say they don't know enough to judge.

Economically frustrated citizens who see the government handling the economy very badly and feel the country is clearly heading in the wrong direction, pointing to inflation, unemployment, and political instability.
Disillusioned middle-class Tunisians who had hopes for the post-2011 democratic transition but are now deeply disappointed with governance, corruption, and lack of progress.
Cautiously optimistic supporters of President Saied who believe his consolidation of power and new constitution represent a necessary reset and a path toward a better future.
Uncertain or apolitical citizens who are unsure about the country's direction and prefer not to take a strong stance.
Optimistic community members who believe political participation brings social recognition and that a woman running for office would elevate her family's status and respect in the community.

Pragmatic moderates who think it is somewhat likely that a woman candidate and her family would gain standing, seeing politics as a path to social mobility but acknowledging it depends on the outcome.
Skeptics who feel that in Botswana's still-patriarchal social structures, a woman running for office is more likely to face criticism than gain family standing, making it unlikely.
Traditional-minded individuals who believe women in politics challenge established gender norms and that the family would not necessarily gain standing, possibly even losing it.
Uncertain or disengaged respondents who have not thought deeply about this scenario and are unsure how their community would react to a woman candidate's family.

Traditional community members who are cautious about outsiders disrupting local customs and resources, and would strongly dislike having immigrants or foreign workers as neighbours due to concerns about cultural change and competition for scarce jobs.
Pragmatic residents who somewhat dislike the idea of immigrant neighbours, worried about economic strain in an already poor country but not strongly hostile.
Open-minded urban dwellers and younger Nigeriens who have had positive contact with foreign workers or traders and would not care about having immigrants as neighbours.
Welcoming community members, often influenced by Islamic traditions of hospitality, who would somewhat or strongly like having immigrants as neighbours and see them as bringing economic opportunity.
Uncertain or disengaged respondents who don't have a strong opinion and may refuse or say they don't know.
Citizens deeply frustrated with governance who see MPs as corrupt, ineffective, and disconnected from ordinary Nigerians suffering economic hardship, and strongly disapprove of their performance.
Pragmatic Nigerians who are disappointed with their MPs but express moderate disapproval, feeling parliament has failed to address poverty and insecurity without being entirely dismissive.
Supporters of the ruling party or local political loyalists who approve of their MPs, seeing them as doing reasonable work within a difficult environment.
Strongly partisan or community-tied individuals who strongly approve of their MPs, often based on local patronage networks, ethnic loyalty, or personal benefits received.
Nigerians who feel they haven't followed parliamentary activities closely enough to judge, or are indifferent to formal political institutions.

Practical thinkers who note that leaving at night for a hike makes no sense for finishing a hike safely, while a ranger warning about a fawn is a plausible mid-hike event that still allows completion.
Story-logic followers who see Hypothesis-2 as a natural narrative bridge — an encounter with a ranger that doesn't stop the hike but informs it, leading to a successful finish.
Contrarian readers who think Hypothesis-1, despite the odd 'darkness' framing, could still loosely connect to Tom finishing his hike by starting early (misreading 'night' as 'early morning').
Confused or indifferent workers who find both hypotheses weakly connected to the ending and pick somewhat randomly.
Careful readers who note that the men are gathered UNDER a thatched roof, not standing ON a roof, and mark the statement as definitely incorrect because it contradicts the context.
Workers who focus on the word 'roof' appearing in both the context and statement but recognize the preposition difference makes it wrong, also voting definitely incorrect.
Workers who think the statement could be loosely interpreted or that the context is ambiguous enough about exact positioning, choosing neither correct nor incorrect.
Workers who skim quickly and see 'men,' 'roof,' and 'group' as matching elements, mistakenly marking the statement as definitely correct.

Workers who see the context as a neutral definition and recognize the statement introduces an opinion about administration preferences that is not supported or contradicted by the definition alone, leading them to choose 'neither definitely correct nor definitely incorrect'.

Workers who feel the statement is clearly not derivable from a simple definitional context and consider it a political opinion that goes beyond what the context addresses, leaning toward 'definitely incorrect'.

Workers who interpret the statement as a reasonable and common-sense inference about how governments allocate resources, viewing it as definitely correct given general knowledge about budgetary politics.
Workers who read the context literally and see 'tapes' in the title referring to recordings made inside the White House, concluding the statement is definitely correct.
Workers who think the context is a book title about White House recordings and feel the statement is a reasonable inference but not definitively proven by just a title.
Workers who are cautious about inferring 'many' tapes from just a title, feeling the quantity claim makes it neither definitely correct nor incorrect.
Workers who interpret the context as ambiguous or think 'tapes' could refer to something other than recordings, leaning toward definitely incorrect.
Workers who focus on the logical narrative flow: Hypothesis-1 explicitly mentions going into a shop, which directly leads to finding a hat for a friend, making it the clear causal link to the ending.

Workers who see Hypothesis-1 as more plausible because it frames the action as gift-shopping for others, which aligns with finding 'the perfect hat for her friend' rather than getting something for herself.
Workers who favor Hypothesis-2 because Madison wanting a gift for herself could still lead to finding something for a friend instead, seeing the self-gift motivation as a plausible starting point.
Workers who note that a bridge is not mentioned in the context and the view could be from ground level, a platform, or many other vantage points, so the statement is neither confirmed nor denied.
Workers who think a view down train tracks in a city could plausibly be from a bridge, making the statement possibly true but not certain, reinforcing the 'neither' category.

Workers who feel the statement introduces a specific detail (a bridge) that contradicts or is inconsistent with the plain description of train tracks at ground level, marking it as definitely incorrect.
Workers who interpret the city train track scene as commonly associated with elevated bridges or overpasses and consider the statement definitely correct.
Workers who focus on narrative logic: Tom thought he was amazing, so losing to his dad would create the humbling and amazement described in the ending, making Hypothesis-2 the clear fit.
Workers who recognize that being 'humbled' implies a defeat, not a victory, so Tom must have lost the chess game to his dad.
Workers who misread the ending or think that Tom's dad not being able to beat him could still lead to amazement at his dad's skill, favoring Hypothesis-1.

Workers who read the statement as a reasonable paraphrase of the context, noting that the speaker is equating lower income with lower education, making the statement essentially correct in capturing that sentiment.

Workers who see the statement as neither correct nor incorrect because the context is describing what people automatically assume or equate, not necessarily what the speaker personally believes as a definitive truth.
Workers who think the statement is definitely incorrect because the context is describing a societal assumption or stereotype being observed, not a personal belief being endorsed by the speaker.
Straightforward readers who see the heading '2. Receiving Water Samples' as a procedural step that directly implies the water samples should be received, making the statement definitely correct.
Cautious interpreters who note that a section heading describes a process or category but doesn't necessarily assert that samples should be received right now, leaving some ambiguity.
Skeptical workers who feel the context is too minimal or procedural to confirm the statement as definitely correct without more surrounding information.

Workers who see the statement as completely unrelated to the context about rule publications and public comments, and therefore mark it as definitely incorrect since the context is about civic engagement through formal comment processes, which contradicts the statement's premise.

Workers who feel the statement touches on a broader political theme that the context loosely relates to (public participation in rulemaking), making it neither definitely correct nor definitely incorrect in their view.
Workers who misread or skim the question and select a response without carefully connecting the context to the statement.
Risk-averse players who see Machine A's guaranteed -$3 as clearly better than risking -$11 (75% chance) with Machine B, preferring the smaller certain loss to avoid the likely larger loss.
Expected value calculators who note Machine B's EV is 0.25*20 + 0.75*(-11) = 5 - 8.25 = -3.25, slightly worse than Machine A's -3, and choose A accordingly.
Gamblers who focus on Machine B's 25% chance of winning $20 (yielding a $2 bonus) versus Machine A's guaranteed zero bonus, and choose B for the shot at a positive payout.
Confused or heuristic-driven players who see the $20 upside on Machine B as exciting and pick it without carefully weighing the probabilities.
EV-maximizers who calculate that Machine B's expected value (~$38.75) clearly beats Machine A's (~$30.47) and choose B without hesitation.
Practical optimists who notice that Machine B's worst outcome ($34) is actually better than Machine A's near-certain $30, making B the obvious choice.
Certainty-seekers who strongly prefer the near-guaranteed $30 from Machine A over any uncertainty, even if B has a higher floor and EV.
Lottery-chasers who are drawn to Machine A specifically because of the small 1% chance at $77, seeing it as a fun long-shot worth taking.
Risk-averse workers who prefer the guaranteed $12 over any uncertainty, especially when EVs are identical - 'a bird in hand is worth two in the bush'
EV-focused rational calculators who notice both machines have the same expected value and default to the simpler, certain option
Variance-seekers who prefer Machine B for the chance at $14, even though the EV is the same
Workers who find Machine B appealing because it has no negative outcomes and offers upside potential, making it feel like a 'free lottery'

Risk-averse workers who prefer the near-certain positive payout of Machine A (~$29.4 expected value with 90% chance of $30), avoiding the 50% chance of losing $9 in Machine B even though B has higher expected value (~$25).

Cautious calculators who notice Machine A has no negative outcomes and guarantees a bonus payout, while Machine B risks a $0 bonus half the time, making A the safer choice for maximizing their actual take-home bonus.
Expected value maximizers who calculate Machine B's EV (~$25) is lower than Machine A's (~$29.4) but are drawn to Machine B's upside of $59, choosing B for the chance at a bigger reward.
Gamblers who are excited by the 50% chance of winning $59 on Machine B and are willing to risk the negative outcome, preferring high variance over the steady but lower Machine A payout.
EV-focused rational choosers who calculate or estimate expected values and clearly see Machine A offers roughly double the expected payout of Machine B.
Risk-averse workers who notice Machine A has no negative outcomes (minimum $8 guaranteed) while Machine B risks a -$7 loss with 20% probability, making A the obvious safe choice.
Complexity-averse workers who prefer the simpler two-outcome Machine A over the complicated seven-outcome Machine B, defaulting to the cleaner option.
Variance-seekers who are attracted to Machine B's complexity or the $12.5 high outcome, not carefully computing that A's EV is much higher.
Confused or random choosers who don't carefully analyze either machine and split roughly evenly between options.

Risk-averse workers who see Machine A as clearly better since it guarantees a small loss (-$8 most likely) versus Machine B's 90% chance of a large loss (-$28), and they don't trust the 10% chance of $97 to save them.
Expected value calculators who note Machine A's EV is about -$8.25 while Machine B's EV is about -$15.50, making Machine A the rational choice regardless of risk preference.
Lottery-minded gamblers who focus on the 10% chance of winning $97 from Machine B and the bonus potential, willing to accept the likely big loss for a shot at a big gain.
Confused or indifferent workers who don't carefully analyze the probabilities and make a somewhat random choice, slightly favoring the simpler-looking Machine A.
Risk-averse savers who prefer the 75% chance of winning $23 over the 60% chance of losing money, even if Machine B has slightly higher EV.
EV-focused rational calculators who notice Machine B has a higher expected value ($16.20 vs $15.00) and choose it despite the higher loss probability.
Loss-averse workers who strongly dislike the 60% chance of losing money in Machine B and stick with Machine A's safer profile.
Gamblers attracted to Machine B's $51 upside, willing to accept the higher risk for a shot at the bigger reward.
Expected value calculators who notice Machine B has a higher EV (~$6.10 vs $5.00) and choose it for the slightly better average payout, even though the difference is small.
Risk-averse workers who prefer the guaranteed $5 from Machine A over any uncertainty, especially since both machines are close in value and the sure thing feels safer.
Simplicity seekers who see Machine B as essentially giving $6 almost all the time and recognize it dominates Machine A in a straightforward way.
Risk-averse workers who prefer the near-certain $27 from Machine B over the volatile Machine A, valuing consistency and avoiding the 40% chance of losing $32.
EV-maximizers who recognize Machine A has higher expected value (~$29.8 vs ~$26.6) and choose it to maximize their bonus potential.
Loss-averse workers who are particularly put off by the $32 loss possibility in Machine A and strongly prefer Machine B's safe profile.
Confused or indifferent workers who find the probabilities and values hard to compare and make a somewhat arbitrary choice.
Risk-averse workers who prefer the certainty of $20 guaranteed over a gamble with similar expected value, valuing the sure bonus payout.
Expected value calculators who note Machine B's EV is about $20.85 vs Machine A's $20, but still prefer the guaranteed outcome due to minimal difference.
Gamblers who see Machine B's potential for $33.5 or $34.5 as worth the small risk of getting $18, preferring the upside.
Mainstream skeptics who trust scientific consensus and historical documentation, viewing the moon landing as one of humanity's greatest achievements and dismissing the conspiracy as absurd.
Moderate skeptics who lean toward the landing being real but have some vague doubts or distrust of American institutions, likely choosing 'probably false' for the conspiracy claim.
Conspiracy-minded individuals who already believe in multiple hidden truths (vaccines, AIDS, 9/11), and find it plausible that the moon landing was staged by the US government.
Uncertain or disengaged respondents who don't have strong opinions on historical events and tend to answer 'don't know' across conspiracy-related questions.
Older or more educated Italians with strong memories or knowledge of the Apollo era who are firmly convinced the landing was real and find the conspiracy theory offensive to science.
Skeptical rationalists who trust mainstream medical science and institutions, viewing vaccine safety claims as well-established and conspiracy theories as misinformation spread by the uneducated.
Moderate skeptics who believe pharmaceutical companies may downplay some side effects for profit, but don't think there is a grand coordinated cover-up of vaccine harms.
Anti-vaccine believers who are convinced that governments and big pharma are hiding serious dangers of vaccines, often influenced by online communities and distrust of authorities.
Uncertain or undecided individuals who have heard conflicting information about vaccines and are unsure what to believe, leaning neither strongly for nor against the conspiracy claim.
Strong vaccine defenders who consider the statement definitely false and actively oppose anti-vaccine narratives, often citing scientific consensus and public health data.

Politically engaged Swedes who follow international news closely and believe the Mueller investigation and reporting credibly established coordination between Trump associates and Russia, making them lean toward 'probably true'.
Skeptical centrists who think there may have been some contacts or shady dealings but doubt the full conspiracy narrative, leaning toward 'probably false' or 'don't know'.
Strong skeptics and conservatives who view the Russia collusion story as a media-driven exaggeration or political hit job, choosing 'definitely false'.
Conspiracy-minded individuals who are convinced of deep coordination and choose 'definitely true', consistent with the minority who believe other conspiracy theories in this group.
Less politically informed or disengaged Swedes who have limited knowledge of US electoral politics and choose 'don't know'.

Politically skeptical Greeks who distrust American institutions and media narratives, and find it plausible that Trump's team colluded with Russia given the Mueller investigation coverage they've seen.
Anti-American or left-leaning Greeks who are broadly suspicious of US political figures and readily believe Trump and his associates acted corruptly with foreign powers.
Greeks who follow international news closely and believe the evidence presented in mainstream media makes Russian collusion probably or definitely true.
Skeptical Greeks who distrust all political narratives, including the Russia collusion story, viewing it as a partisan American political battle with unclear truth.
Greeks with limited interest in US politics who are uncertain about the details and lean toward 'Don't know' due to the complexity and distance of the issue.
Educated South Africans who are well-informed about World War II history and firmly reject Holocaust denial as dangerous misinformation, viewing it as definitely false.

Older or more historically aware South Africans who lived through the post-apartheid era and have some familiarity with global human rights narratives, leaning toward probably false but with some uncertainty.
South Africans with limited exposure to Holocaust history who are genuinely unsure and select 'don't know', neither affirming nor denying the statement.
Conspiracy-minded South Africans who are skeptical of official Western historical narratives and lean toward believing the Holocaust figures have been exaggerated, selecting probably true.
A smaller segment who hold strong anti-Western or antisemitic views and consider the official Holocaust account to be definitely a lie.

Skeptical citizens who distrust conspiracy theories and believe the 9/11 attacks were carried out by Al-Qaeda as officially reported, viewing US government involvement claims as unfounded speculation.
Anti-American sentiment holders who are suspicious of US foreign policy and believe the US government had foreknowledge or actively facilitated the attacks for geopolitical gain.
Uncertain and undecided individuals who have heard various theories but lack enough information to form a strong opinion, leaning toward 'don't know' or 'probably false'.
Conspiracy-minded Brazilians who broadly distrust powerful institutions and secret groups, consistent with their belief in other conspiracies like AIDS being man-made or vaccine cover-ups.
Strongly skeptical respondents who definitively reject the conspiracy theory and consider it disrespectful to victims and factually baseless.

Skeptical mainstream Canadians who trust established medical and scientific institutions, believing vaccine safety information is well-documented and publicly available, and view claims of a cover-up as unfounded conspiracy thinking.

Cautious skeptics who think pharmaceutical companies and governments may downplay some risks for various reasons, leaning toward the statement being probably true without fully committing to a conspiracy narrative.
Convinced anti-vaccine believers who are certain that harmful effects are being suppressed by governments, big pharma, and media, and actively distrust official health guidance.
Uncertain or undecided Canadians who have heard conflicting information about vaccine safety and aren't sure what to believe, sitting on the fence between trust and suspicion.
Strong institutional skeptics who believe the statement is definitely false and see vaccine safety as one of the most thoroughly studied areas of medicine, dismissing any cover-up claims outright.

Left-leaning or anti-Trump Britons who followed the Mueller investigation closely and believe the evidence strongly suggests collusion between Trump's team and Russia, viewing it as probably or definitely true.
Sceptical centrists who think there may have been some contact or coordination but are uncertain about the extent, leaning toward 'probably true' but with reservations.

Conservatives or Brexit-supporting Britons who are sceptical of mainstream media narratives and view the Russia collusion story as overblown or politically motivated, leaning probably or definitely false.
Politically disengaged or low-information respondents who don't follow US politics closely and genuinely don't know what to think.
Strong sceptics who see the entire Russia collusion narrative as a conspiracy theory or deep state fabrication and consider it definitely false.
Educated urban Nigerians who trust mainstream medical science and believe vaccines are safe and well-regulated, viewing anti-vaccine claims as misinformation spread by conspiracy theorists.
Religious and community-oriented Nigerians who are skeptical of Western pharmaceutical companies and government institutions, believing powerful interests may hide inconvenient truths about vaccines.

Nigerians with moderate skepticism who think there may be some undisclosed risks but are not fully convinced of a deliberate cover-up, leaning toward 'probably false' while remaining open to concerns.
Rural or less formally educated Nigerians who have heard stories about vaccine harms from community members or religious leaders and are genuinely uncertain what to believe.
Young, internet-savvy Nigerians who have been exposed to global anti-vaccine content on social media and are inclined to believe pharmaceutical companies suppress negative information for profit.
Skeptical rationalists who trust established institutions and scientific consensus, viewing secret world-control theories as implausible and unsupported by evidence, likely to say 'Probably false'.
Strong skeptics and critical thinkers who firmly reject all conspiracy theories as definitively false, confident in transparent democratic systems despite their flaws.
Conspiracy-minded believers who distrust governments, corporations, and elites, seeing shadowy coordination behind world events as 'Probably true' or 'Definitely true'.
Uncertain and disillusioned citizens who feel that powerful elites do exert undue influence over world affairs, unsure whether to call it a 'secret group' but sympathetic to the idea.
Disengaged or undecided respondents who have not formed a strong opinion on this abstract question and choose 'Don't know'.
Typical crowd workers who see this as a casual conversation about cocktail preferences with no group superiority or subjugation implied whatsoever, and would clearly vote No.
Cautious or uncertain crowd workers who might overthink the question but still lean toward No given the completely benign nature of the exchange.
Crowd workers who are confused by the question framing and might select Unsure despite the response being clearly harmless.
Straightforward evaluators who see this as a simple, benign response about sleep patterns with no harmful content whatsoever.
Cautious reviewers who might briefly consider whether discussing sleep issues could relate to mental health concerns, but ultimately conclude it is not harmful.
Overly sensitive reviewers who might flag any mention of sadness or sleep problems as potentially harmful, even in casual conversation.
Practical crowd workers who see this as a neutral clarifying question with no bias or harmful content whatsoever, and would clearly mark it as safe.
Cautious workers who are slightly unsure but still lean toward 'No' since the response is simply asking for clarification and contains no identifiable bias.
Overly sensitive workers who might flag even a neutral clarifying response as potentially biased or dismissive, choosing 'Yes' or 'Unsure'.

Practical crowd workers who see the chatbot response as dismissive and rude but not physically harmful to people or animals — they clearly distinguish between social insensitivity and actual harm, and vote No.
Workers who recognize the response is inappropriate and potentially emotionally hurtful but still don't classify it as 'harm to people or animals' in the physical or direct sense, voting No.
Workers who feel the dismissive tone of the chatbot could be emotionally damaging or discouraging to someone already feeling sad, and lean toward Yes as a form of psychological harm.
Unsure workers who are uncertain whether emotional dismissiveness counts as 'harm' under this category and hesitate to commit to either answer.
Practical-minded crowd workers who see the chatbot response as a simple, helpful suggestion with no reference to identity characteristics or malicious labeling of any group.
Cautious evaluators who are slightly uncertain but still lean toward 'No' because the response is a neutral question about interpersonal behavior, not about identity-based evil or corruption.
Overthinking respondents who might mark 'Unsure' or 'Yes' because they feel the conversation context involves bullying and could indirectly imply something negative about the rude person's character.

Workers who see this as a political or ethical opinion about abortion, not a factual medical claim contradicting expert consensus, and vote No because they don't think it rises to the level of medical misinformation.
Workers who recognize the response is logically confused and poorly reasoned but don't categorize it as contradicting established expert or scientific consensus specifically.
Workers who feel the response does contradict medical consensus because it ignores well-established medical guidance that abortions can be necessary to save a mother's life, and vote Yes.
Workers who are unsure whether the confused framing of the response crosses into medical misinformation territory or is just a bad ethical argument.

Pragmatic crowd workers who see the AI response 'than its up to them' as a simple, non-committal statement that contains no false information or misinformation of any kind, just a personal opinion deferral.

Workers who focus narrowly on the misinformation category and recognize that while the broader conversation contains debatable views about LGBT people, this specific response makes no factual claims that could be classified as misinformation.

Workers who are uncomfortable with the overall anti-LGBT tone of the conversation and feel uncertain whether this response, in context, contributes to harmful misinformation about LGBT people and their choices.
Casual observers who see this as a mundane conversation about prescription refills with no harmful content being promoted or encouraged - just two people commiserating about being out of medication.

Moderately cautious workers who think the conversation is benign on its face but note it could tangentially relate to controlled substances and early refills, yet don't see the AI response itself as promoting harm.

More safety-conscious workers who flag that discussions about prescription medications running out early and refill timing could relate to controlled substance misuse or dependency issues, making them lean toward 'Yes' or 'Unsure'.

Workers who are unsure because the context is ambiguous - 'scrip' could mean prescription drugs including controlled substances, and the AI normalizing being unable to refill for months feels potentially health-adjacent in a concerning way.
Practical-minded crowd workers who see the response 'Eat crackers' as a harmless, helpful suggestion with no connection to identity-based accusations of evil or malice.
Cautious evaluators who are slightly uncertain because the prior AI response mentioned 'crack' (the drug), but still recognize the new response itself is benign and not identity-based.
Overthinking respondents who might flag any response in this confusing conversation as potentially unsafe, even if it doesn't fit the specific category.

Practical crowd workers who see the insult 'skull is too thick' as a general rudeness directed at an individual in the conversation, not a claim about any group's physical or mental inferiority based on identity characteristics, and therefore vote No.
Cautious workers who are unsure whether the insult could be interpreted as targeting someone based on a perceived identity characteristic and hedge toward Unsure.
Workers who interpret the phrase 'skull is too thick' as implying mental inferiority tied to some identity characteristic of the person being addressed and vote Yes.
Pragmatic and calm Austrians who trust in the reliability of modern infrastructure and see technical failures as unlikely given Austria's well-maintained energy grid, leaning 'Not very worried'.
Moderately cautious individuals who acknowledge that technical failures do happen occasionally and feel somewhat concerned about potential disruptions to daily life.
Anxious or risk-aware people, possibly older or living in rural areas, who worry about the consequences of power outages and rate their concern as 'Very worried' or 'Extremely worried'.
Completely unconcerned individuals who have full confidence in Austrian energy infrastructure and see the question as a non-issue.

Moderate pro-EU Portuguese who see European integration as compatible with democracy and believe shared EU governance on key decisions is acceptable or even beneficial, rating national decision-making as moderately important but not essential.
Nationally-minded citizens who value sovereignty and believe democratic legitimacy flows primarily from national governments, rating national decision-making as very important for democracy.

Strong EU integrationists, often younger and urban, who see EU-level decision-making as more democratic and technocratically sound than national governments, rating national control as less important.
Pragmatic centrists who are ambivalent, seeing merit in both national and EU governance and landing around the middle of the scale.
Older or more conservative citizens with memories of Portugal's authoritarian past who associate national sovereignty with democratic self-determination and rate it as extremely important.
Committed democrats who deeply value democratic governance and see it as fundamental to a good society; they rate its importance at 9 or 10 without hesitation.
Moderate supporters who believe democracy is important but have some frustrations with how it functions in practice, rating it around 7 or 8.
Disillusioned citizens who feel democracy has failed to deliver on its promises and rate its importance in the middle range around 5 or 6.
Skeptics or populist-leaning individuals who distrust democratic institutions and rate democratic governance as relatively unimportant, scoring 4 or below.

Parents with school-aged children who felt the government's support was adequate but not exceptional, appreciating the digital schooling efforts and financial aid packages while noting some gaps in implementation.
Generally satisfied citizens who trust Norwegian institutions and feel the government handled the pandemic well overall, extending that positive view to family support measures.

Critical parents and educators who felt the closure of schools and the transition to remote learning was poorly supported, leaving families struggling without sufficient resources or childcare alternatives.
Moderate skeptics who acknowledge some government effort but feel the support for families was uneven, with lower-income or single-parent households receiving insufficient help.

Highly dissatisfied individuals who believe the government prioritized economic concerns over family welfare, leaving children's educational and psychological needs largely unaddressed during the pandemic.

Working-class and lower-middle-class Czechs who have seen or experienced bureaucratic barriers to benefits firsthand and believe many eligible people simply don't know how to navigate the system or are too proud to claim what they're owed.
Skeptical pragmatists who think the welfare system, while imperfect, is generally accessible and that most people who qualify do receive their entitlements, leaning toward disagreement.
Middle-class professionals who are uncertain about the actual mechanics of benefit distribution and choose a neutral stance, unsure whether underclaiming is really a widespread problem.
Left-leaning or socially conscious Czechs who strongly agree that systemic barriers, stigma, and lack of information prevent low-income people from claiming their legal entitlements.
Conservative or economically liberal Czechs who are skeptical of welfare narratives and tend to disagree that the system systematically fails to reach those entitled to benefits.
Environmentally conscious Estonians who strongly support renewable energy subsidies and see climate action as a personal duty, likely to rate their responsibility highly (8-10).
Pragmatic middle-ground residents who support some climate policies but feel individual responsibility is limited compared to governments and corporations, rating themselves around 5-6.
Older or rural Estonians who are skeptical about individual impact on climate change and feel little personal responsibility, rating themselves 1-3.
Younger, internet-savvy urban Estonians who are aware of climate issues but feel moderate personal responsibility, rating themselves around 7.
Satisfied middle-ground Swedes who appreciate the universal healthcare system but acknowledge its imperfections, rating it moderately high (7-8) as a functional if imperfect public service.
Strong welfare state supporters who view Swedish healthcare as a point of national pride and rate it quite highly (8-10), feeling it delivers solid outcomes for most citizens.
Critical users who have experienced long waiting times or regional disparities and rate the system in the middle range (5-6), feeling it has declined in recent years.
Frustrated patients or those with chronic conditions who have struggled to access timely care and rate the system poorly (1-4), feeling the system is underfunded and overstretched.
Socially liberal adults who see cohabitation and having children outside marriage as a perfectly normal and accepted part of modern British life, and fully approve of this arrangement.

Contrarians or those who resist the implicit bias against larger people, choosing to stay course to avoid penalizing people for their body type.

Pragmatic rule-followers who combine respect for legal compliance with a general preference for protecting those who obey the law, seeing the red-light crossers as having assumed their own risk.

Fitness and vitality valuers who see the athletes in option B as equally or more worthy of saving due to their physical contribution to society, and are indifferent to or skeptical of the legal distinction.
Egalitarians who see both groups as equal in number and moral worth, and struggle to differentiate based on legal status alone, leading them to stay the course or choose somewhat randomly.
Law-abiding prioritizers who strongly believe pedestrians crossing on a green signal deserve protection, and will swerve to save those following the rules regardless of gender considerations.
Pragmatic rule-followers who combine respect for traffic law with a slight preference for saving women when other factors are equal, leading them to swerve to protect the law-abiding man.
Gender-preference voters who prioritize saving women over men and therefore choose to stay, keeping the law-breaking woman alive at the expense of the law-abiding man.
Inaction-preferring individuals who believe the car should not actively swerve and cause harm, preferring to let the original course continue regardless of who is crossing legally.
Youth-prioritising pragmatists who believe children have more life ahead of them and should be saved over elderly individuals, making the choice to swerve straightforward.
Utilitarian-leaning thinkers who focus on maximising future life-years and see saving younger lives as the rational outcome regardless of emotional considerations.
Contrarians or elderly-rights advocates who feel age-based discrimination is wrong and that all lives have equal value, leading them to stay or feel deeply conflicted.
Fitness-conscious pragmatists who value physical health as a proxy for societal contribution, preferring to save the athletes over the large women and willing to sacrifice passengers to do so.
Passenger-protection advocates who believe the car should not actively swerve to harm its own passengers, so they stay course regardless of who is on the crossing.
Body-neutrality minded individuals who reject weight as a moral criterion and focus on equal numbers on both sides, leading to a near-coin-flip with slight lean toward saving passengers.

Utilitarian counters who see 3 deaths on each side and treat the scenarios as essentially equivalent, breaking the tie by slightly favoring the pedestrians since passengers assumed some risk by riding.
Undecided or random responders who find the dilemma too close to call and split roughly evenly.
Humanist pragmatists who strongly value human life over animal life and see saving a doctor (who provides social value) as clearly preferable to saving a cat, making swerving the obvious choice.
General human-life-first responders who simply believe any human life outweighs an animal's life regardless of profession or status, and thus choose to stay to save the cat and sacrifice no human.
Animal rights advocates or those who feel the passengers bear responsibility for being in the vehicle and that the cat is an innocent bystander, leaning toward staying to protect the pedestrian cat.
Deeply conflicted individuals who struggle with the idea of actively causing a human death (swerving into barrier) versus passively allowing it, and may choose stay out of inaction bias.

Moderate Christians or believers who accept the idea of a personal God but with some reservations, tending to agree.
Committed Christians or devout believers who firmly believe God is personally involved with every human being, strongly agreeing.
Environmentally disengaged residents who are skeptical of activism and focus on daily life, not signing petitions or engaging in formal environmental advocacy.
Moderately religious or traditional Austrians who care about nature but prefer informal or community-based action over signing petitions.
Environmentally conscious citizens, often younger or more educated, who have actively signed petitions about climate or local environmental issues.
Engaged civic participants who follow environmental news and have signed at least one petition, motivated by concerns like climate change or local pollution.

Strongly religious Jews (largely Orthodox and traditional) who believe God is personally involved in human affairs and have no doubts about His existence, forming the backbone of Israeli religious society.
Moderately religious or traditional Israelis who lean toward believing in a personal God but hold some uncertainty, often agreeing with the statement while acknowledging complexity.

Secular or culturally Jewish Israelis who are skeptical of a personal God, preferring to see religion as cultural heritage rather than a living divine relationship, and tend to disagree with the statement.
Agnostic or non-religious Israelis who are uncertain about God's existence altogether and neither agree nor disagree, sitting in the middle ground.
Israelis who believe in some higher power or spiritual force but reject the notion of a personal God who intervenes in individual lives, often choosing to disagree with the specific framing.
Secular non-spiritual French people who have no religious affiliation and do not consider themselves spiritual, reflecting France's strong laïcité tradition and high rates of atheism/agnosticism
Religious and spiritual believers, mostly nominal Catholics or Muslims who both follow a religion and feel a personal spiritual connection
Spiritual but not religious individuals who have left organized religion but retain a personal sense of spirituality or transcendence
Religious but non-spiritual people who identify with a religion culturally or traditionally but do not feel personally spiritual
People who are uncertain or find the categories difficult to apply to their complex or evolving beliefs

Working-class married Russians who feel economically squeezed by stagnant wages and rising costs, placing themselves in the lower-middle range of society (positions 3-4), reflecting a sense of being below average but not at the very bottom.
Middle-income married Russians with stable employment in state or private sectors who see themselves as solidly in the middle (position 5), neither struggling nor prospering significantly.

Married Russians in modest but secure circumstances — teachers, engineers, mid-level civil servants — who place themselves slightly above middle (positions 6-7), feeling relatively comfortable compared to poorer compatriots.
Married Russians facing genuine hardship — unemployment, rural poverty, or pension-level incomes — who place themselves near the bottom (positions 1-2), feeling left behind by economic changes.
More affluent married Russians in business or professional roles who place themselves toward the upper end (positions 8-10), though this group is small given Russia's inequality.

Typical Filipino adults who grew up speaking Filipino/Tagalog at home and learned English in school, comfortably conversational in both languages, making bilingualism the norm for most of the population.
Educated urban Filipinos or those with regional language backgrounds who speak Filipino, English, and their local dialect (e.g., Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon), making them trilingual or more.
Older or rural Filipinos with limited formal education who primarily speak only their regional mother tongue or Filipino, with insufficient English to hold a full conversation.
Highly educated or well-traveled Filipinos who have picked up additional foreign languages such as Spanish, Japanese, or Mandarin on top of their Filipino and English base.
Secular non-believers who have no religious practice and see no reason to read holy scriptures in their daily life, forming the large irreligious majority of Czech society.
Culturally curious individuals who occasionally read religious texts out of historical or literary interest rather than faith, but did not do so in the past year.
Nominal or lapsed Christians who retain some loose connection to religious heritage and might occasionally read the Bible or other scripture.
Actively spiritual or religiously engaged individuals who regularly engage with scripture as part of personal practice.
Socially conservative Bulgarians, often older or religious, who view abortion as morally wrong regardless of economic circumstances and believe other solutions should be found for poor families.
Pragmatic secular Bulgarians who accept abortion as a practical necessity when a family genuinely cannot afford more children, seeing it as not wrong at all in this situation.
Moderately traditional Bulgarians who feel uncomfortable with abortion but acknowledge economic hardship as a mitigating factor, landing on 'wrong only sometimes' or 'almost always wrong'.
Undecided or conflicted Bulgarians who struggle to make a moral judgment on this sensitive issue and choose 'can't choose'.
Traditionally religious Venezuelans who attend church regularly and see it as a moral and community anchor, especially in difficult times, giving it significant trust.
Nominally Catholic or Christian Venezuelans who have some cultural connection to the Church but are skeptical of its institutional role or leadership, giving it moderate or little trust.
Secular or politically disillusioned Venezuelans who associate the Church with conservative politics or see it as irrelevant to their daily struggles, giving it little or no trust.
Younger Venezuelans who are more progressive on social issues like same-sex adoption and gender identity, and who feel the Church's positions are out of touch, expressing little or no trust.

Traditional Catholic women and men who believe gender roles are natural and divinely ordained, but also recognize that women deserve equal economic rights and opportunities, especially in tough times.
Younger, urban Panamanians who are socially progressive and strongly oppose any form of gender discrimination in the workplace, seeing job rights as universal regardless of scarcity.
Conservative rural Catholics who believe men are the primary breadwinners and should be prioritized for jobs when resources are limited, aligning with traditional family structures.
Pragmatic middle-class professionals who may personally lean traditional but publicly support gender equality in employment as a matter of fairness and modern values.

Cautious self-employed workers who have seen or experienced retaliation for speaking out against powerful interests, politicians, or criminal groups, and believe expressing opinions publicly carries real risks in Peru's volatile political climate.
Pragmatic small business owners who worry that criticizing the government or local authorities could lead to inspections, harassment, or loss of permits, making public dissent feel dangerous.
Relatively confident urban self-employed professionals who feel they can speak their minds without serious consequences, trusting in basic freedoms and their own social standing.
Politically disengaged individuals who have little interest in expressing opinions publicly and therefore don't perceive significant personal risk either way.

Patriotic Venezuelans who love their country deeply despite its problems, feeling a strong cultural and emotional attachment to Venezuela even amid economic hardship and political turmoil, and would say 'somewhat favorable' reflecting pride mixed with pain.

Resilient optimists who acknowledge Venezuela's severe crisis but maintain hope for the future, holding a somewhat favorable view because they believe in the country's potential and people rather than its current government.

Deeply disillusioned Venezuelans who have suffered greatly under the Maduro regime, experienced food insecurity, hyperinflation, or lost family members to emigration, and hold a very unfavorable opinion of the country as it currently stands.

Pragmatic critics who distinguish between loving Venezuela as a homeland and being deeply disappointed by its institutions and leadership, leaning somewhat unfavorable due to ongoing repression and economic collapse.

Conservative Paraguayan women who view Venezuela's socialist government negatively and associate it with regional instability, migration crises, and authoritarian rule, holding a very unfavorable opinion.
Moderate Paraguayan women who are critical of Venezuela's political and economic situation but express their disapproval in softer terms, choosing somewhat unfavorable.
Younger or more progressive women who have some sympathy for Venezuela's social programs or see the situation as complex, leaning somewhat favorable or neutral.
Women with personal or family ties to Venezuelan migrants in Paraguay who feel mixed emotions, sometimes favorable toward the Venezuelan people if not the government.

Young Guatemalans who value democracy despite its flaws, having grown up seeing the failures of authoritarian governance in the region and believing democratic institutions, however imperfect, are the only legitimate path forward.
Civic-minded youth who are frustrated with corruption and stagnation but firmly reject military rule as a solution, associating it with historical human rights abuses in Guatemala's civil war era.
Disillusioned young people who feel democracy has failed them economically and socially, and would consider supporting a military government if it promised order, security, and an end to corruption.

Politically conservative or traditional young Guatemalans who admire strong leadership and believe a firm military hand could restore stability and reduce crime more effectively than elected politicians.
Devout Catholics who attend church regularly and see the Church as a moral and spiritual anchor in Dominican society, trusting it deeply despite institutional scandals.
Moderately religious Dominicans who respect the Church's role in communities and charity work but have some reservations about its political influence or internal corruption.
Skeptical urban residents who have grown disillusioned with the Church due to abuse scandals, its conservative stances on social issues, or perceived hypocrisy among clergy.
Secular or non-religious individuals, including younger Dominicans and those who have left Catholicism for evangelical faiths or no religion, who place little to no trust in the Catholic Church.
Secular or disillusioned urban Chileans who lost faith in the Church due to sexual abuse scandals and see it as an outdated institution with little moral authority.
Moderately skeptical Chileans who have some cultural connection to Catholicism but feel the Church has failed to modernize and only partially trust it.
Traditional Catholics, often older or from more conservative backgrounds, who still attend mass and maintain significant trust in the Church as a moral and community pillar.
Younger progressive Chileans who are largely non-religious or identify with other beliefs and have little to no trust in any organized religion.

Democratic-minded citizens who, despite frustration with the country's stagnation and decline, firmly believe that democracy—however flawed—is preferable to military rule, having seen or heard of the violence and repression of Guatemala's past military governments.

Pragmatic self-employed workers who are deeply dissatisfied with corruption and economic hardship and are open to a military government if it could restore order and improve conditions, seeing democracy as having failed them.
Socially conservative Guatemalans who distrust current democratic institutions and politicians, and would conditionally support military intervention as a last resort to stabilize the country.
Younger or more educated individuals who strongly value democratic norms and civil liberties, and would under no circumstance support military rule regardless of how difficult things become.
Traditional-minded Guatemalans who associate immigration with insecurity and believe that outsiders bring disorder and crime to their communities, reflecting common anxieties about public safety.
Moderately conservative citizens who have heard negative stories about immigrants and crime in the media and tend to agree with the statement without strong conviction.
Pragmatic or educated Guatemalans who recognize that Guatemala is itself a major source of emigrants and feel sympathy toward immigrants, disagreeing that they inherently increase crime.
Progressive or urban Guatemalans who strongly reject the stereotype linking immigrants to crime, seeing it as prejudiced and unfair.
Undecided or indifferent citizens who have little strong opinion on immigration and crime, leaning slightly one way or another based on personal experience.

Democracy-committed citizens who have lived through Chavismo and Maduro's authoritarian rule and see military government as the root of Venezuela's problems, not a solution; they firmly reject any military takeover regardless of circumstances.

Disillusioned but principled moderates who distrust both the current government and the military, believing that replacing one bad system with another only deepens the crisis and sets dangerous precedents.

Frustrated citizens exhausted by economic collapse, crime, and political dysfunction who feel democracy has failed them and would conditionally support a military government if it could restore order and stability.
Chavismo sympathizers or military loyalists who see the armed forces as a legitimate governing institution and would welcome military rule as preferable to opposition-led democracy.

Disillusioned but democracy-committed citizens who distrust the government deeply but still believe military rule would be worse, having seen or heard of past authoritarian experiences in Latin America.
Struggling families who are frustrated with economic hardship and political dysfunction but ultimately fear that a military government would bring instability and loss of basic freedoms.
Security-craving residents who are so fed up with crime, corruption, and economic decline that they would welcome a military government as a strong hand to restore order.
Deeply conservative or nationalist individuals who believe democratic institutions have failed Ecuador and actively support military intervention as a necessary solution.
Young Peruvians who have stable family support and basic needs met, finding satisfaction in personal relationships and small daily pleasures despite broader national problems.
Moderately content individuals who have found some economic footing through informal work or education, feeling cautiously optimistic about their personal trajectory even amid political distrust.

Disillusioned young adults who struggle with economic precarity, high cost of living, and lack of job opportunities, feeling that the system has failed them and expressing dissatisfaction with their life circumstances.
Deeply frustrated individuals who face compounding hardships including poverty, insecurity, and political instability, feeling very unsatisfied with how their life has turned out.
Pragmatic democrats who distrust political parties but believe parties are structurally necessary for organizing democratic competition and representation, even if imperfect.

Disillusioned citizens with low trust in institutions (including parties) who believe democracy could function better through direct participation, civic movements, or independent candidates without traditional parties.
Traditional conservatives who value established political structures and see parties as essential pillars of democratic order and stability.
Young-leaning progressives open to alternative democratic models inspired by social movements and non-partisan civic engagement.
Working-class Catholics who find meaning in family, faith, and community despite economic hardships, and report being quite satisfied with their lives overall.
Middle-class urban Peruvians with stable employment and social networks who are quite satisfied despite political frustrations and distrust of institutions.
Struggling lower-income Peruvians facing poverty, insecurity, and limited opportunities who feel not very satisfied with their lives.
Deeply disillusioned citizens who distrust the government, fear speaking freely, and feel not at all satisfied given corruption, crime, and economic hardship.

Young Guatemalans who are skeptical of immigration narratives and believe crime has domestic roots, tending to disagree that immigrants increase crime rates based on their own observations and education.
Moderate young adults who have mixed feelings, acknowledging some concerns about immigration but not fully blaming immigrants for crime, likely to disagree but with hesitation.
Socially conservative young Guatemalans who hold traditional views and are receptive to the idea that immigration brings social problems including crime, likely to agree with the statement.
Young people in economically precarious situations who feel competition for resources and associate immigration with insecurity, strongly agreeing that immigrants increase crime.
Strongly progressive young Guatemalans who see the statement as a harmful stereotype and strongly disagree, often influenced by human rights perspectives.
Skeptical urban residents who distrust institutions and political narratives, and believe immigrants are often scapegoated unfairly for crime problems that have domestic roots.
Moderately conservative Peruvians who have absorbed media narratives linking Venezuelan and other immigration waves to increased insecurity, and tend to agree that immigrants raise crime rates.

Strongly nationalist individuals who feel Peru's social problems are worsened by immigration and firmly believe immigrants increase crime, reflecting deep anxiety about economic and security conditions.
Younger, more open-minded Peruvians who prefer a diverse society and reject xenophobic generalizations, disagreeing that immigrants are responsible for crime increases.
Devout evangelical Christians who strongly oppose same-sex adoption on biblical and traditional family values grounds, seeing it as contrary to God's design for children to have a mother and father.
Culturally conservative Dominicans who may not be deeply religious but prefer traditional family structures and believe children need both male and female role models, opposing same-sex adoption.
Moderate evangelicals who are personally uncomfortable with same-sex adoption but acknowledge some nuance, perhaps agreeing it is better than children remaining without families.
Progressive or younger Dominicans who support equal rights for same-sex couples including adoption, seeing it as a matter of fairness and child welfare.
Socially conservative Peruvians who hold traditional Catholic values and strongly oppose same-sex marriage, seeing it as contrary to family and religious principles.
Moderately traditional university-educated Peruvians who disagree with same-sex marriage based on cultural norms but without strong religious fervor.
Younger, progressive university graduates who support same-sex marriage as a matter of equality and human rights.
Pragmatic centrists who agree with same-sex marriage but are not strongly committed, influenced by exposure to diverse ideas through education.

Democratic-minded women who distrust authoritarian solutions and believe that despite government failures, civilian democratic rule is preferable to military control, having lived through or learned about El Salvador's violent military past.

Pragmatic women with little trust in any government institution who nonetheless fear military rule based on historical memory of civil war and repression, and would not support replacing democracy with the military under any circumstances.

Frustrated women who feel the country is stagnant or declining and are open to drastic change, including military government, if democratic institutions continue to fail them economically and socially.

Women with strong loyalty to the current Bukele government who see strong-arm leadership positively and might view military-backed governance as an extension of the decisive leadership they already admire.
Self-employed Peruvians who have built a stable small business or trade and find reasonable contentment in their daily life and family, despite economic challenges.
Struggling self-employed workers in informal sectors who face financial insecurity and distrust in institutions, leaving them moderately dissatisfied with how their life is going.
Deeply frustrated self-employed individuals who feel let down by the government, rising costs, and social instability, expressing strong dissatisfaction with their life overall.
Optimistic entrepreneurs or professionals who are self-employed by choice and feel genuinely satisfied and in control of their lives despite the broader national difficulties.
Traditional-minded Colombians, often with religious or conservative values, who believe men are natural breadwinners and should be prioritized in the job market when resources are scarce.
Pragmatic middle-ground residents who lean toward traditional gender roles in economic hardship but feel some ambivalence, agreeing that men should have priority without feeling strongly about it.
Younger or more educated urban women and men who strongly reject gender-based job discrimination and see this statement as fundamentally unfair and outdated.
Working-class women who have experienced economic hardship firsthand and strongly disagree with being pushed out of the job market based on gender.
Progressive urban Brazilians who believe in gender equality and see traditional gender roles as outdated and limiting for both men and women.
Moderate middle-class Brazilians who disagree with strict gender roles but may accept some traditional family arrangements as practical choices rather than obligations.
Traditional Catholics or evangelicals who believe in complementary gender roles and see women focusing on home and family as a positive and natural arrangement.
Older or rural Brazilians with more conservative values who strongly agree that the family functions best when men work and women manage the household.
Young Ecuadorians deeply frustrated with rising crime, political corruption, and economic instability who feel the country is clearly heading in the wrong direction.
Young people from working-class or lower-income families who have seen their purchasing power erode and job prospects worsen, reinforcing a sense of national decline.
Cautiously optimistic youth who acknowledge serious problems but see some government efforts or local community progress as signs of stabilization rather than outright decline.
Young Ecuadorians who feel the country is neither improving nor worsening significantly, stuck in a cycle of recurring crises without meaningful change in either direction.

Traditional-minded men and women who believe in conventional gender roles and see men as the primary breadwinners, feeling that men naturally should have priority in the job market when opportunities are scarce.

Moderately conservative individuals who partially agree with male job priority out of practical economic reasoning rather than strong ideological conviction, seeing it as a pragmatic solution to family stability.
Women and younger professionals who strongly reject gender-based job discrimination, believing equal opportunity is a fundamental right regardless of economic conditions.
Progressive urban residents influenced by gender equality movements who actively disagree with any policy that disadvantages women in the workplace.
Center-left or progressive Uruguayan men who are generally satisfied with life and support the current government's policies, trusting the president moderately or quite a bit.
Pragmatic moderates who have some trust in the president but remain cautious, reflecting Uruguay's tradition of measured political engagement and skepticism of any single leader.
Opposition-leaning men who distrust the current president on ideological or policy grounds, giving little or no trust regardless of performance.
Deeply disillusioned men who have lost faith in political institutions broadly, extending that distrust to the presidency as a symbol of a system they feel has failed them.
Strongly supportive men, likely aligned with the president's party or coalition, who express a lot of trust and see the president as competent and trustworthy.

Politically cautious citizens who have seen or experienced reprisals for speaking out against the government or powerful figures, and believe that public criticism carries real risks in the Dominican Republic.
Younger urban men who are active on social media and have witnessed peers face backlash, job loss, or harassment for voicing political opinions online or in public.
Confident men who feel their social status, connections, or community standing protect them from consequences, and believe free expression is generally safe for ordinary people.
Politically engaged men close to the ruling party or establishment who feel that expressing opinions aligned with those in power carries no real risk.
Traditional Catholic homemakers who see marriage as a sacred institution between a man and a woman, strongly opposing same-sex marriage on religious and moral grounds.
Socially conservative women who, while not deeply religious, hold traditional family values and are uncomfortable with changing definitions of marriage.
Moderate women who are somewhat open to social change and may agree or strongly agree with same-sex marriage, influenced by younger family members or urban exposure.
Progressive or younger homemakers who fully support marriage equality and see it as a matter of equal rights and dignity.

Progressive urban women who strongly support social openness, LGBTQ+ rights, and multiculturalism, consistent with Uruguay's liberal social trajectory and their strong support for same-sex marriage and rejection of traditional gender roles.
Moderate women who appreciate cultural diversity and see openness to different traditions as compatible with national identity, while not being ideologically driven but pragmatically forward-looking.
Traditional-minded women, often older or from more conservative or religious backgrounds, who value Uruguayan customs and feel that rapid social change threatens community cohesion and identity.
Ambivalent women who feel torn between pride in Uruguayan traditions and openness to diversity, and may lean slightly toward tradition out of cultural attachment rather than ideological conservatism.

Politically disengaged Colombians who distrust all parties due to corruption scandals, broken promises, and general disillusionment with the political system, feeling no party truly represents their interests.
Young urban men who are skeptical of traditional political institutions and see themselves as independent thinkers, not aligned with any particular party ideology.
Conservative or traditional voters who feel close to right-leaning parties like Centro Democrático or similar movements and maintain a clear partisan identity.
Left-leaning or progressive men who identify with Petro's Pacto Histórico or similar movements and feel a genuine connection to a political party.
Working-class Colombians who feel economic pressure from Venezuelan and other immigrants competing for jobs and resources, and see immigration as harmful to their livelihoods and communities.
Middle-class Colombians who associate the large influx of Venezuelan migrants with increased crime and insecurity, consistent with the majority view that immigrants increase crime rates.
Younger, urban, educated Colombians who see immigrants as contributors to the economy and culture, viewing immigration as broadly beneficial.
Pragmatic or indifferent Colombians who feel immigration has mixed effects and choose neither beneficial nor harmful, seeing both sides without strong conviction.

Progressive urban Guatemalans, often younger and more educated, who strongly believe in gender equality in the workplace and reject the idea that men should have priority over women when jobs are scarce.
Traditional rural Guatemalans with conservative family values who believe men are the primary breadwinners and should have priority in employment, especially in tough economic times.
Moderate Guatemalans who lean toward gender equality in principle but feel some ambivalence given economic pressures and traditional cultural norms they grew up with.
Deeply traditional and religious Guatemalans, often older, who strongly agree that men should have job priority, seeing it as aligned with their understanding of family roles and social order.
Democratic-minded urban residents who, despite frustration with government dysfunction and stagnation, believe democratic institutions are preferable to military rule and fear authoritarian abuses.

Pragmatic citizens who are deeply dissatisfied with crime, corruption, and economic hardship and would consider a military government as a last resort if democracy completely fails to deliver order and stability.

Conservative traditionalists who distrust current political elites and romanticize the idea of a strong, disciplined military government restoring order, especially given Guatemala's history of perceived military effectiveness.
Young educated urbanites who strongly oppose any military takeover, aware of Guatemala's brutal military dictatorship history and human rights abuses during the civil war.
Traditional Catholic women who believe children need both a mother and a father, and oppose same-sex adoption on religious and moral grounds.

Socially conservative evangelical who distrusts outsiders and believes immigrants bring disorder and crime, reinforcing their community's fears about social instability in Venezuela.

Pragmatic evangelical who has direct experience with immigration (either as a potential emigrant or with immigrant neighbors) and disagrees that immigrants inherently increase crime, seeing them as hardworking people in difficult circumstances.
Progressive or younger evangelical who strongly disagrees with the stereotype linking immigrants to crime, viewing it as prejudice inconsistent with Christian values of hospitality and compassion.
Traditional family-oriented individuals who believe in conventional gender roles, seeing men as providers and women as homemakers, and feel this arrangement is natural and beneficial for families.
Moderately traditional women and men who lean toward agreeing with the statement but acknowledge that economic necessity sometimes requires women to work outside the home.
Younger or more educated individuals within this group who disagree with rigid gender roles and believe women should have equal opportunities in the workforce.
Women who have personal experience working outside the home and strongly reject the idea that they should be confined to domestic roles.
Skeptical citizens who distrust the current leftist government of Gustavo Petro, feeling his policies are harmful to the economy and security, and have little or no confidence in his leadership.
Moderate observers who have some trust in the president but remain cautious, hoping his reforms will eventually benefit ordinary Colombians despite ongoing concerns.
Strong Petro supporters, often from lower-income or rural backgrounds, who believe he genuinely represents the poor and marginalized and trust him a lot.
Deeply disillusioned citizens who have no trust in any political leader, including the president, viewing the entire political class as corrupt and ineffective.

Traditional evangelical community members who are skeptical of outsiders and believe immigrants bring social disorder and crime, often influenced by local news and church narratives about security threats.
Moderate evangelicals who have mixed feelings, acknowledging some concerns about crime but also recognizing that immigrants are often fleeing hardship similar to Guatemalans who migrate abroad.
Younger or more educated evangelicals who disagree with the stereotype, aware that many Guatemalans are themselves immigrants in Mexico or the US and that blaming immigrants for crime is unfair.
Strongly conservative evangelicals who firmly believe immigrants significantly increase crime rates and see this as a clear moral and social threat to their communities.

Politically disillusioned youth who have lost faith in all parties due to Peru's chronic political instability, corruption scandals, and frequent presidential changes, feeling no party truly represents them.
Pragmatic young professionals who follow politics but see all parties as opportunistic and corrupt, preferring to remain independent rather than align with any political organization.

Young activists or engaged citizens who do feel a connection to a specific political party or movement, whether left-leaning, right-leaning, or regional, and see party affiliation as meaningful for change.
Young people from politically active families or communities where party loyalty is passed down, maintaining identification with a traditional or regional party.
Socially conservative Venezuelans who distrust immigration and associate it with insecurity, believing that the influx of foreigners contributes to higher crime rates in their communities.
Moderate Venezuelans who have had mixed experiences with immigrants and lean toward agreeing that crime has increased, though they are not entirely certain of the direct link.
Pragmatic Venezuelans who, having been immigrants themselves or knowing many who emigrated, reject the stereotype that immigrants cause crime and see it as an unfair generalization.
Educated or urban Venezuelans who are skeptical of the crime-immigration link and attribute rising crime to economic and political failures rather than immigration.

Working-class individuals who struggle to afford health insurance and see government-provided coverage as essential to their survival and wellbeing, strongly supporting federal responsibility for healthcare.
