Fiscally conservative individuals who worry about government overreach and dependency, believing healthcare is a personal responsibility rather than a federal obligation.
People with mixed or ambivalent views who support some government role but are uncertain about full federal responsibility, torn between practicality and concerns about government efficiency.
Center-right married Americans who believe in personal responsibility and limited government, feeling that Washington overreaches into areas better handled by private enterprise and individuals.

Moderate married Americans who are skeptical of government efficiency but acknowledge some role for government in solving big societal problems, landing somewhere in the middle but leaning toward less government.
Progressive-leaning married Americans who see government as a necessary tool to address inequality, healthcare, education, and other systemic issues that the market fails to fix.
Married Americans in working-class or economically vulnerable situations who personally rely on or have relied on government programs and believe government should do more to help people like them.

Moderate religious Americans who feel the U.S. is sometimes taken advantage of in trade and international relations, and believe other countries don't always reciprocate fairly in diplomacy or economics.
Patriotic churchgoers with a somewhat skeptical view of globalism and international institutions, feeling that the U.S. gives more than it gets in foreign aid and alliances.

Younger or more educated religious attendees who see international relations as complex but broadly fair, and are skeptical of narratives about America being victimized.

Younger, globally-minded never-married adults who follow international news and see trade and diplomacy as generally reciprocal, believing the US both benefits from and contributes fairly to global relationships.
Progressive-leaning singles who are skeptical of nationalist narratives and feel claims of being 'taken advantage of' are often exaggerated or politically motivated.

Working-class or economically anxious never-married adults who feel trade deals and foreign competition have hurt American workers and that other countries exploit US generosity or military protection.
Politically moderate singles who are uncertain but lean toward believing some countries do take advantage of the US, particularly on trade, influenced by recent debates over China and tariffs.
Middle-class retirees who worked in private sector jobs and diligently saved through employer-sponsored 401K plans or opened IRAs, seeing these accounts as essential to their retirement security.

Higher-income professionals and business owners who maximized contributions to multiple retirement accounts over their careers and have substantial savings.

Secular progressives who see organized religion as a force that opposes LGBTQ rights, reproductive rights, and social justice, viewing churches as net negative institutions in public life.

Progressive people of faith who see their church communities as genuinely positive forces for social good, emphasizing service to the poor and community building.
Pragmatic liberals who separate institutional religion from personal faith and believe many churches do meaningful humanitarian work, viewing their effect as broadly positive.

Faith-driven welcoming Christians who emphasize biblical teachings on hospitality to strangers and see immigrants as enriching American society and their congregations.

Religious and community-minded conservatives who prefer private charity and local solutions over federal government programs, seeing government aid as counterproductive
Religiously conservative patriots who feel America is taken advantage of in trade and foreign policy, and believe other nations don't reciprocate fairly in international dealings.
Traditional values churchgoers who are skeptical of globalism and international institutions, feeling the U.S. gives more than it receives on the world stage.
Moderate religious attendees who see international relations as generally reciprocal and believe America is treated fairly by most allies and trading partners.
Younger or more globally minded congregation members who attend services frequently but hold more nuanced views on international fairness and diplomacy.
Deeply religious Black Christians who see faith in God as central to morality and community life, viewing belief as essential to being a good person.

Fiscal conservatives who believe college education is a personal investment and responsibility, not a government entitlement, and worry about the cost to taxpayers.
Traditional conservatives who value self-reliance and the free market, seeing federal involvement in higher education as overreach that would reduce quality and increase dependency.
Moderate conservatives or younger conservatives who are sympathetic to college affordability concerns and might support some federal role, though perhaps not full provision.

Moderate centrists who are frustrated with both parties and see value in some government programs but worry about overreach and inefficiency.

Fiscally conservative independents who may support some social programs but fundamentally believe government is too large and intrusive in economic matters.

Traditional-values Catholics who see immigration as a cultural threat, often older and more conservative, worried that American customs and Christian heritage are being diluted by large numbers of newcomers.

Progressive and social-justice-oriented Catholics who embrace the Church's teachings on welcoming the stranger and see immigrants as enriching American society culturally and economically.
Hispanic and immigrant-background Catholics who personally identify with the newcomer experience and strongly believe immigration strengthens America.
Younger Catholics who are more cosmopolitan and open to diversity, viewing cultural change as positive and seeing immigration as part of America's historical identity.

Pragmatic progressives who see college access as increasingly necessary for economic participation and believe the government should help level the playing field, similar to how they view housing as a federal responsibility.
Working-class individuals without college degrees who feel left behind and support government-funded education as a way to give future generations better opportunities than they had.
Fiscally cautious moderates who support some social programs but draw the line at college, seeing it as a personal choice and investment rather than a universal right the government should fund.

Libertarian-leaning skeptics who distrust government involvement in education, worry about costs and inefficiency, and believe individuals and families should bear responsibility for higher education.

Culturally conservative Black Americans who hold traditional values and worry that rapid demographic and cultural change threatens the established American way of life they identify with.

Protestants who are skeptical of financial institutions or who rely primarily on Social Security, pensions, or church community support for retirement security.

Middle-class and upper-middle-class workers in the Northeast with stable careers who have employer-sponsored 401K plans or have set up IRAs, seeing retirement savings as a standard part of financial planning.
Self-employed professionals, small business owners, or freelancers in the region who have proactively opened IRAs or solo 401Ks to manage their own retirement savings.
Lower-income workers, part-time employees, or younger adults in the Northeast who lack access to employer retirement plans and cannot afford to contribute to an IRA.
Older residents who are already retired and may have cashed out or no longer actively hold a retirement account, or who relied on pensions instead.

Secular progressives who strongly support social safety nets and believe government assistance is essential for lifting people out of poverty, consistent with their support for bigger government and federal health care responsibility.

Established professionals and academics with stable careers who have been contributing to employer-sponsored 401K plans or personal IRAs for years as part of standard financial planning.
Mid-career postgraduate degree holders who set up retirement accounts early and continue to maintain them, viewing them as essential financial tools.

Individuals who are self-employed, between jobs, or in non-traditional career paths who lack access to employer-sponsored plans and have not set up independent retirement accounts.
Civil liberties-minded independents who see voting as a cornerstone of democracy and are wary of restrictions that could disenfranchise legitimate voters, especially minorities and the poor.
Pragmatic centrists who believe voting is a right but also think some basic verification measures are reasonable, yet still lean toward the 'fundamental right' framing when forced to choose.
Security-focused independents who worry about election integrity and believe that attaching some responsibilities or requirements to voting is a fair and reasonable standard.
Disengaged or conflicted independents who are unsure where they stand on voting rights versus election security and may refuse or answer inconsistently.

Libertarian-leaning conservatives who oppose government intervention in personal decisions and therefore support abortion remaining legal even if they find it distasteful.
